title: Why a Swamp Cooler Makes Your House Dustier
metaTitle: Why a Swamp Cooler Makes Your House Dusty
metaDescription: Evaporative coolers bring outdoor air into the house. Learn where dust collects, what to clean first, and when the cooler itself needs HVAC service.
summary: A swamp cooler continually brings in outdoor air, so cleaning works best when you start near the airflow and finish with the floors.
transcript: An evaporative cooler works by pulling hot outdoor air through wet pads and blowing the cooled air into the house. It isn't a closed system. While refrigerated air mostly recirculates indoor air through a filter, a swamp cooler keeps bringing in a fresh supply from outside.

That design works well in our dry climate, but it also means outdoor dust has a direct path into the house. A clean, intact pad catches some debris, but it isn't the same as a central HVAC filter. Windy weather, worn pads, dirty louvers, gaps around the unit, and dusty ductwork can all make the difference more noticeable.

Most evaporative coolers also need an exhaust path. That usually means partially opened windows or dedicated up-ducts, depending on the system. If your house uses open windows, the sills and tracks near those openings will collect dust too.

Start with the supply vents and the horizontal surfaces closest to them. Turn the cooler and ceiling fans off while you work. Wipe the accessible vent face, then use a barely damp microfiber cloth on nearby shelves, furniture, and trim. Dry dusting puts the finest material back into the air.
Clean ceiling fan blades before anything below them. Dust on the blades stays out of sight until the fan starts, then spreads across the room you just finished.
Next, vacuum window tracks and loosen the corners with a soft brush. Follow with a damp cloth. Don't flood the track because standing water can reach drywall, wood trim, or the wall below it.

Fabric holds dust longer than hard surfaces. Vacuum upholstery and rugs with the attachment the manufacturer recommends, and wash curtains or bedding according to their care labels. If hard surfaces look dusty again soon after cleaning, soft furnishings may still be releasing what they collected.
Do the floors last. Vacuum first, then damp mop tile or other washable hard flooring. Change the water when it turns cloudy so you aren't spreading fine grit from one room to the next.

The cooler itself is HVAC work. Las Cruces Cleaning doesn't service rooftop units, pads, pumps, belts, water lines, or ductwork. If the dust level changes suddenly, debris blows from a vent, the air smells musty, or the pads have heavy mineral buildup, have the system inspected instead of trying to reach into it from the roof or duct.
localNote: Evaporative cooling makes sense in the Mesilla Valley because it works best in dry air. The tradeoff is a steady connection to outdoor conditions, including our windy spring weather. Clean according to what you can see and feel in the house, and shorten the interval during dusty weeks instead of following the same schedule all year.

faq.q: Does a swamp cooler make more dust than refrigerated air?
faq.a: It can. Refrigerated air mostly recirculates indoor air through a filter, while an evaporative cooler continually draws from outside. The difference depends on wind, pad condition, ductwork, and how the house exhausts the incoming air.

faq.q: Should I close the windows to stop the dust?
faq.a: Not unless your system has another approved exhaust path, such as up-ducts. A typical evaporative cooler needs somewhere for the incoming air to leave. Follow the cooler manufacturer's instructions or ask an HVAC technician how your system is designed.

faq.q: Why does the dust feel gritty?
faq.a: Desert soil and mineral residue can both feel gritty, but texture alone can't tell you the source. If grit appears directly below a vent or the amount changes suddenly, have the cooler and ductwork checked.

faq.q: How often should we clean during cooler season?
faq.a: Start with visible surfaces once a week and a fuller clean every two weeks, then adjust to the house. Wind, open windows, pets, flooring, and the cooler's condition matter more than the calendar.
